To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
selective punishment of inter-response times can increase the rate of responding and can eliminate responding.
selective punishment of long interresponse times can increase or decrease the rate of responding, depending on the shock intensity and the range of interresponse times punished.
the selective suppression of long interresponse times is possible with a range of shock intensities and that shock intensity can affect response rate and interresponse time.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of selective punishment contingencies on the interresponse times of rats responding on a multiple fixed-ratio schedule of food presentation, with the aim of identifying the conditions under which selective punishment of the long interresponse times produces response-rate increases.
the effects of shock parameters and scheduling on the behavior maintained by variable-interval schedules.
the development of procedures that can be used to study the control of the temporal patterning of operant behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
selective interresponse-time punishment schedules are effective in reducing the targeted interresponse times, but that response-rate increases may not occur.
shock intensity and scheduling are important factors to be considered in the study and application of selective interresponse time-dependent punishment procedures.
selective punishment of inter-response times is a function of both the shock intensity and the scheduling of shock delivery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

selective interresponse-time dependent shock schedules are effective in producing response-rate increases, and in suppressing the targeted interresponse times, when the shock intensity is low and the interresponse-time target is broad.
the selective targeting of interresponse times is a robust phenomenon, although the response-rate effects are variable.
selective punishment of long interresponse times produces differential suppression of the target responses but does not necessarily increase response rates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of shock intensity and shock schedule are not independent of one another, but rather interact to produce the effects observed.
shock intensity is an important variable to consider when designing selective interresponse-time schedules.
selective ITI-dependent punishment schedules can be used to increase response rate, but only under certain circumstances.
